name: Multi-Region Disaster Recovery
description: A pattern for deploying workloads across multiple geographic regions to survive complete regional outages. Provides the highest level of resilience for critical national infrastructure and services where regional failure would have significant public impact.
whenToUse: Critical national infrastructure where regional failure is unacceptable
Services with 99.99% or higher availability requirements
Workloads where regulatory requirements mandate geographic redundancy
Services where a complete regional outage would have significant public or economic impact
Disaster recovery scenarios requiring recovery within minutes rather than hours
whenNotToUse: Most government services where multi-AZ provides sufficient resilience
Services where the cost of multi-region deployment is disproportionate to the risk
Workloads with data residency requirements restricting deployment to a single region
Applications that cannot tolerate eventual consistency between regions
Services with low traffic where the complexity of multi-region is unjustified

typicalComponents.name: Global Load Balancer
typicalComponents.purpose: Route traffic to the nearest healthy region with automatic failover
typicalComponents.technology: Route 53, Azure Traffic Manager/Front Door, or Cloud DNS

typicalComponents.name: Regional Application Stacks
typicalComponents.purpose: Independent application deployments in each region
typicalComponents.technology: ECS/EKS, App Service, or GKE per region

typicalComponents.name: Cross-Region Database Replication
typicalComponents.purpose: Replicate data between regions for DR or active-active operation
typicalComponents.technology: Aurora Global, Cosmos DB, or Cloud Spanner

typicalComponents.name: Cross-Region Storage Replication
typicalComponents.purpose: Replicate objects and files between regions
typicalComponents.technology: S3 Cross-Region Replication, GRS, or Multi-Region Storage

typicalComponents.name: DR Orchestration
typicalComponents.purpose: Automate failover procedures and validate recovery readiness
typicalComponents.technology: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, Azure Site Recovery, or custom runbooks

securityControls: Ensure encryption keys are available in all deployment regions
Implement consistent IAM policies and access controls across regions
Ensure security monitoring covers all regions with centralised alerting
Validate that data replication complies with data residency requirements
Implement network security consistently across regional deployments
Test security controls work correctly after regional failover
resilienceConsiderations: Active-active provides highest availability but requires conflict resolution for writes
Active-passive is simpler but has non-zero RTO during failover
Pilot light keeps minimal infrastructure warm in DR region to reduce recovery time
Cross-region replication introduces latency — design for eventual consistency
Regular DR testing (game days) essential to validate failover procedures
Consider the RPO implications of asynchronous cross-region replication
costConsiderations: Multi-region effectively doubles or triples infrastructure costs for active-active
Active-passive with pilot light reduces standby costs significantly
Cross-region data transfer costs can be substantial for high-volume replication
Global database services (Spanner, Cosmos DB) have premium pricing
Factor in the cost of regular DR testing and validation exercises
Weigh the cost against the financial impact of extended regional outage
operationalConsiderations: Deployment procedures must coordinate releases across multiple regions
Monitoring must provide global visibility with per-region drill-down
DR runbooks must be documented, tested, and kept current
Regular DR exercises (at least quarterly) to validate recovery procedures
Capacity planning must account for full traffic in each region during failover
Team must understand the consistency model and its implications for users

questionsToAsk: What is the target RTO and RPO for regional failure scenarios?
Is active-active or active-passive the appropriate DR strategy?
Are there data residency constraints on which regions can be used?
How frequently will DR failover be tested?
What is the acceptable data loss window for asynchronous replication?
Who has authority to invoke regional failover and what is the decision process?
commonMistakes: Implementing multi-region without regular DR testing, discovering failures only during real incidents
Assuming synchronous replication across regions — latency makes this impractical for most workloads
Not accounting for DNS TTL propagation time in failover RTO calculations
Deploying multi-region for services that don't justify the cost and complexity
Not considering data consistency implications when both regions accept writes
